text: A dictionary that will take fifteen years to compile, and a young man in a publishing house who is better with words than with people. Majime is put on the team behind The Great Passage, and the film takes the work itself seriously: the index cards, the arguments over a single definition, the paper stock chosen so a thumb can separate one leaf from the next. Ishii gives this 133 minutes, which is the point — the pace belongs to a project measured in decades, not quarters. Around the desks the office ages, colleagues leave, deadlines slip, funding wobbles. What the film watches is the strange loyalty a person can develop toward an object no one is waiting for, and the slow discovery that a man who cannot say what he means to a woman has spent his life cataloguing exactly the words that would let him.

Two Jewish brothers, one who stayed in the East and one who went West, are told by their mother's will that they must live under one roof before either sees a mark of it. Levy sets this in a reunified Germany where the old border still runs through the family arithmetic — a hustler with debts on one side, an observant household on the other, and a shiva that has to be performed by people who barely know the choreography. Ninety-one minutes, farce timing, doors and lies. The comedy comes from the specific business of getting through a week: kosher rules improvised, a pool tournament that will not wait, a wife counting what is left. That German audiences of 2004 could laugh at this together was itself part of what the film was doing.

Two men are thrown out of their villages for being unbearable musicians, which is how they end up in a forest meeting the king of ghosts. He gives them three wishes. Ray, working in Bengali with songs and a kingdom at war, makes a children's fantasy that is also a plain-spoken argument about armies: Halla is marching on Shundi, and the two least qualified people in the region hold the only power that might stop it. The ghost dance is stagecraft of a kind rarely attempted anywhere in 1967. What gives the film its footing is that the magic never makes Goopy and Bagha competent — they remain exactly who they were, hungry and easily impressed, wandering into a war with a drum and a voice.

A mining company wants the uranium under a stretch of Australian desert. The Aboriginal men sitting on that ground say it is where the green ants come to dream, and that waking them ends the world. Herzog stages the collision as a legal one, which is stranger than a violent one would be: surveyors, geologists, a courtroom in which two entirely incompatible accounts of what land is must be entered into a record designed for only one of them. He shoots the flat country with the patience of someone who suspects the argument is already lost. The German title is what he named it, though the film is made in and about Australia — an outsider's picture, and it knows it, which is why the company men are given their reasonableness intact.

Kirishima quits the volleyball team and vanishes, and he never appears on screen. What Yoshida films instead is the school in the days afterward: the girlfriend, the second-string player suddenly promoted, the film club kids in the corner who were never in his orbit at all. The same afternoon is replayed from different desks, so that a moment which meant nothing from one angle turns out to have been the whole day from another. This is a high-school picture with no adult crisis and no lesson, and its subject is the invisible ranking every corridor runs on — who gets looked at, who does the looking. The absent boy works as pure pressure. Everyone rearranges around a hole, and discovers what they were actually standing on.

Three hours with a family that has not been in the same room for years. Glasner gives the Lunies four names and lets each one carry a long stretch of the film alone: Lissy the mother, Gerd the father, Tom conducting an orchestra through a piece he is not sure is any good, Ellen drinking through a job in dentistry. They are estranged in the ordinary German way, by geography and by nobody making the call. Illness is what reassembles them, and the film refuses to make that reunion tender — the funniest scenes are also the cruellest, and a hospital corridor produces the kind of laughter that comes from exhaustion. At 182 minutes it has room for scenes that a shorter cut would have called unnecessary. Those turn out to be the ones that land.

A mother and daughter are sealed into an apartment by a quarantine order, and the walls are covered in blue plastic sheeting because the building is being repainted. Chung Mong-hong made this in Taiwan in 2021, close enough to the event that the confinement needs no explanation, and he uses the blue as light — an aquarium glow that turns a normal flat into somewhere underwater. The mother is a manager with a marriage behind her and a job that is thinning out. The daughter has her own school year to lose. What the film tracks is which of them is actually coming apart, and how long the other takes to notice, and it is careful to make the answer a matter of household logistics: who cooks, who pays, who leaves the room.
